The ten Kihon Kumite are universal across Wado bodies (Otsuka left them unstandardised, so the sequences differ between organisations, but all teach them). NOT flagged disputed: the parenthetical is doing real work here because 'Kihon Kumite' unqualified would collide with generic basic sparring drills in other styles.

meaning: bright mirror / polished mirror
name: Meikyo
note: Held (line 92). No originator known for the parent Rohai. The condensation of three kata into one is a substantive Shotokan modification, not a renaming. Funakoshi's rename of Rohai ('vision of a heron'); the Shotokan form condenses Itosu's three Rohai into one kata, a reworking generally associated with Gigo Funakoshi, and includes the distinctive sankaku-tobi triangular jump. Tetsuhiko Asai later added Meikyo Nidan and Sandan in his JKS lineage. Renamer: Gichin Funakoshi. New characters: 明鏡, 'bright mirror' or 'polished mirror', for the opening triangular hand form, with the deliberate allusion to the mirror of Amaterasu and to the Zen sense of polishing the mind. What changed: the Shotokan form is not any one of Itosu's three Rohai but an amalgam of them, condensed and reworked by Gigo, which is why it does not match the Rohai of Matsubayashi-ryū or Shitō-ryū. name: Sochin (Shotokan)
note: The Shotokan Sochin differs so extensively from Aragaki Seisho's Naha/Tomari Sochin (kept in Shito-ryu) that it is treated as Gigo Funakoshi's creation, exemplifying his deep-stance, powerful reform of Shotokan. Gichin Funakoshi's proposed Japanese rename Hakko never displaced the old name. The clearest single example of the distinction the client wants. Gichin attempted the renaming, to Hakkō, and it failed; Gigo did the technical work, and it stuck. Gigo brought the Aragaki-line Sōchin into Shotokan while studying Shitō-ryū material, and rebuilt the whole kata on fudō-dachi, the rooted stance now called sōchin-dachi after it, in place of the Shitō-ryū nekoashi-dachi and zenkutsu-dachi. The result is close to a new kata sharing an embusen with its parent. Record Gichin as attempted renamer (name rejected) and Gigo as modifier, not as creator, since the source kata is Aragaki's. meaning: 'Kata of heaven' (or 'of the universe'): part of a projected heaven-earth-man (ten-chi-jin) series of which only 'heaven' was completed, expressing fundamentals as the root of everything above them.

name: Ten no Kata
note: A wartime training innovation in two halves: omote, performed solo, and ura, performed with a partner, making it one of the first Japanese karate kata designed explicitly around paired application. Development is generally attributed to Gigo Funakoshi under his father's name; it remains central in Shotokai and is preserved in parts of Shotokan. The second outright creation, and structurally unlike any Okinawan kata: Ten no Kata 天の形, 'form of the heavens', is in two halves, omote performed solo as a basics drill and ura performed with a partner as prearranged kumite. It is a bridge from kihon to kumite invented for the university teaching programme, not a transmitted form, and Funakoshi's own text specifies fudō-dachi for many of the blocks, which is itself a marker of Gigo's technical vocabulary. Kept by the Shotokai as a Funakoshi legacy form; not in the JKA syllabus. Note that Funakosh

Funakoshi altered the stance from the Okinawan pigeon-toed naihanchi-dachi to the wider kiba-dachi, so the Korean form descends from a form already once modified. meaning: 'Righteous discipline' or right rhythm. Second-degree black belt form; 82 movements.

note: MISSING from the database. The higher ATA black-belt forms (Chung San, Sok Bong, Chung Hae, Jhang Soo, Chul Joon, Jeong Seung) complete the 18-form system and are omitted here as the client asked for the ATA only in brief. Level not verified against an ATA source in this session.
provenance: Original ATA composition.

era: Created 1965-1967 with the Palgwae; adopted 1967 and retained after 1972
meaning: 'Diamond', from the Buddhist Vajra, meaning that which is hard and indestructible. Named for Mount Kumgang, the most celebrated mountain in Korea, and for the Keumgang Yeoksa, the guardian warriors carved at temple gates. The performance line traces the hanja 山 (mountain).
name: Keumgang
note: CORRECTION and DISPUTE. The database dates this to 1967 but credits Lee Chong-woo, who did not join the committee until 1971. The yudanja poomsae were the work of the 1965-67 six-man group; Lee Chong-woo and the Ji Do Kwan / Moo Duk Kwan members arrived only for the Taegeuk revision. Kukkiwon does not itself name authors, so all individual attributions here are reconstructions from participant testimony. Second-dan Kukkiwon poomsae from the original KTA black-belt set. Second of the nine black-belt poomsae.
provenance: Original KTA composition. Second dan poomsae. Unlike the Palgwae, the yudanja set survived the 1972 revision.

meaning: 'Foundation forms'. Three elementary I-pattern forms teaching low block, middle punch and stance turning; the Korean counterpart of the Shotokan Taikyoku series.
name: Kicho Hyung
note: Modelled on the Taikyoku kata of Shotokan, which the kwan founders learned in Japan or from Funakoshi's books; Hwang Kee formalised them as Ki Cho Hyung Il Bu, E Bu and Sam Bu in the Moo Duk Kwan. Most kwans used equivalents as first-geup forms before the Pyung Ahn series. Basic series taught before the Pyung Ahn.
origin_person: Gichin Funakoshi and Gigo Funakoshi (Taikyoku model); adapted by Hwang Kee and Won Kuk Lee
origin_place: Tokyo, Japan; adapted in Seoul, Korea
variants: Ki Cho Hyung Il Bu / E Bu / Sam Bu

era: Modelled on Taikyoku Nidan; Korean version from the mid-1940s
meaning: 'Basic form, part two'. As part one but with the punches delivered at high level.
name: Kicho Hyung Ee Bu
note: MISSING as an individual entry. Same transmission dispute as Kicho Hyung Il Bu. [Verifier: Same as Il Bu: Taikyoku Nidan modelling is inferred from close resemblance, while Hwang Kee claimed original authorship. Note the inconsistency that Gigo Funakoshi is dropped from introduced_by here but present for Il Bu. disputed=true must stay.] Second of the three basic forms.
origin_person: Gichin and Gigo Funakoshi (model); adapted by Hwang Kee
provenance: DERIVES FROM Taikyoku Nidan, brought across by Won Kuk Lee from Funakoshi's Shotokan and adopted in parallel by Hwang Kee.
sources: Hwang Kee, Tang Soo Do (Soo Bahk Do), 1978

era: Modelled on Taikyoku (c. 1936-1940); Korean version taught from the mid-1940s
meaning: 'Basic form, part one'. A teaching form of front stance, low block and lunge punch on the I-shaped embusen.
modified_era: Late 1940s to 1950s, fixed in Hwang Kee's 1958 and 1978 manuals
name: Kicho Hyung Il Bu
note: MISSING as an individual entry: the database holds only a combined 'Kicho Hyung'. DISPUTED. How Hwang Kee obtained the Shotokan forms is the central unresolved question of Tang Soo Do history. Hwang claimed transmission from the Chinese master Yang Kuk-jin in Manchuria plus independent study; Won Kuk Lee claimed Hwang had been his student at Chung Do Kwan, which Hwang denied; a third account has Hwang learning the kata from Funakoshi's books in the Korean railway library where he worked. The Taikyoku forms themselves are usually credited to Gichin Funakoshi but were in practice devised by his son Gigo, which is a second layer of dispute. [Verifier: Form exists and the Taikyoku derivation is  Hwang Kee's basic form, modelled on Taikyoku/Kihon.
origin_person: Gichin Funakoshi and Gigo Funakoshi (Taikyoku Shodan model); Korean version adapted by Hwang Kee
provenance: DERIVES FROM Taikyoku Shodan. Carried across by Won Kuk Lee, who trained under Funakoshi at Shotokan in Tokyo, and independently adopted by Hwang Kee from Funakoshi's published texts.
sources: Hwang Kee, Tang Soo Do (Soo Bahk Do), 1978
Kidokwan, 'Quest for the Truth: The Origin of Tang Soo Do's Forms'

era: Modelled on Taikyoku Sandan; Korean version from the mid-1940s
meaning: 'Basic form, part three'. Introduces the back stance and inside-outside block.
name: Kicho Hyung Sam Bu
note: MISSING as an individual entry. Same transmission dispute. [Verifier: Same as Il Bu and Ee Bu: derivation from Taikyoku Sandan is inferred, Hwang Kee's own account contradicts it, and Won Kuk Lee's 'brought' role rests on a transmission claim Hwang Kee explicitly rejected.] Third of the three basic forms.
origin_person: Gichin and Gigo Funakoshi (model); adapted by Hwang Kee
provenance: DERIVES FROM Taikyoku Sandan, via the same double route.
sources: Hwang Kee, Tang Soo Do (Soo Bahk Do), 1978

era: 1962-1964, Malaysia period; removed from the official 24 c. 1986
meaning: Pen name of the patriot Cho Man-sik (1883-1950), who devoted his life to the independence movement and the education of his people. 39 movements represent his times of imprisonment and his birthplace on the 39th parallel.
modified_era: Removed 1986; restored by the GTF from 1990
modifier: Choi Hong-hi (removed it); Park Jung-tae (restored it in the GTF, 1990)
name: Ko-Dang
note: DISPUTED. Cho Man-sik was a Christian nationalist purged by the North Korean regime, which is widely held to be why Choi removed the pattern once ITF headquarters moved towards Pyongyang; Choi's own stated reason was technical redundancy. Also one of the fifteen patterns claimed by Kim Bok-man. Original member of the Chang Hon set replaced by Juche in the mid-1980s; ironically Cho Man-sik was executed in North Korea, and many non-ITF Chang Hon organisations (and post-2002 ITF branches) still teach Ko-Dang. Replaced by Juche in 1986 in the main ITF line but kept or restored by the GTF and by some ITF branches, so its status as a current requirement is contested.
origin_person: Choi Hong-hi with the Malaysia-period pattern team
provenance: Original Chang Hon composition; still taught in GTF and in several ITF splinter federations.

era: Kata c. 1760s-1800s; in Korea from mid-1940s
meaning: The Korean reading of the Chinese characters 公相君 (Kusanku), the honorific title of a Chinese envoy to Okinawa c. 1756 whose fighting method inspired the kata; the Koreans preserved the older personal name rather than Funakoshi's rename Kanku ('viewing the sky').
name: Kong Sang Koon
note: Transmitted to Korea as Shotokan's Kanku Dai but retained under its Okinawan name in Korean reading; it is the longest and most senior of the classical Tang Soo Do hyung. The story of the envoy Kusanku teaching his art is early tradition recorded in the Oshima Hikki (1762). Korean recension of Kusanku.
origin_person: Kata attributed to Tode Sakugawa, after the envoy Kusanku
origin_place: Okinawa (Chinese influence via Fuzhou); brought to Seoul, Korea

meaning: The Goryeo dynasty (918-1392) and the seonbae spirit of the scholar-warrior who resisted the Mongols. The performance line traces the hanja 士 (seonbi, 'scholar'), signifying the learned man of conviction.
modified_era: 1975 onwards; details clarified in successive Kukkiwon Textbook editions
name: Koryo
note: DISPUTED. Kukkiwon publications present the poomsae as collective committee work and name no individual author; the widespread attribution to Lee Chong-woo personally rests on interviews with his students rather than on KTA minutes. What is documented is the composition of the enlarged 1971-72 committee. The database's current attribution to Lee Chong-woo and Lee Kyo-yoon alone is too narrow. First-dan Kukkiwon poomsae; the 1967 'Original Koryo' created with the Palgwae set was replaced by the present Koryo when the Taegeuk system was adopted, and the older form survives only as a historical curiosity. The entry point of the black-belt curriculum in Kukki taekwondo.
provenance: Original composition. First dan poomsae; note it replaced a same-named 1967 form of entirely different content.

era: 1962-1964, while Choi was ambassador to Malaysia
meaning: Named for Gwanggaeto the Great, 19th king of Goguryeo, who recovered the lost territories including most of Manchuria. 39 movements refer to the first two figures of 391 AD, the year he took the throne; the diagram represents the expansion and recovery of lost territory.
modified_era: Published 1965; revised with sine-wave in the 1983 Encyclopedia
name: Kwang-Gae
note: DISPUTED. Kim Bok-man and Woo Jae-lim state they helped Choi develop fifteen tul between 1962 and 1964 in Malaysia, of which this is one. Choi's own encyclopaedia names no co-authors. The ITF acknowledges 'assistance' from Nam Tae-hi, Kong Young-il, Han Cha-kyo, Choi Chang-keun, Woo Jae-lim, Kim Bok-man and Park Jung-tae across the whole 1955-1988 development, without allocating patterns. The claim is credible but contested and should not be presented as settled either way. First-dan Chang Hon pattern honouring the expansionist Goguryeo king. First of the black-belt tul. Added itf-chang-ung, itf-choi-jung-hwa, itf-weiler, gtf. First dan-grade tul. The nine colour-belt tul carried oh-do-kwan while the fifteen black-belt tul carried nothing beyond itf-taekwondo/taekwondo, which is the split that made the Korean rows look arbitrary. oh-do-kwan is deliberately not extended to the senior tul:
origin_person: Choi Hong-hi with the Malaysia-period pattern team
provenance: Original Chang Hon composition, worked out in Kuala Lumpur during Choi's ambassadorship.

meaning: Named for King Munmu, 30th monarch of the Silla dynasty. 61 movements refer to the last two figures of 661 AD, the year he came to the throne. His body was buried near Dae Wang Am (Great King's Rock) after he asked, in his will, that his body be placed in the sea so that his spirit might for ever defend Korea against Japanese aggression.
name: Moon-Moo
note: DISPUTED: one of the fifteen 1962-64 Malaysia patterns. Historical figure honoured: King Munmu of Silla. [Verifier: Era and team wrong. Moon-Moo is one of the four 1972 additions taking the set from 20 to 24; not a 1962-64 Malaysia creation and not in Kim Bok-man's claimed list.] Fourth-dan pattern noted for its extremely slow, controlled kicks; the underwater-tomb story is Silla legend attached to a real site (Daewangam). Part of the yondan group of Chang Hon tul. Added itf-chang-ung, itf-choi-jung-hwa, itf-weiler, gtf. Fourth-dan tul.
origin_person: Choi Hong-hi with the Malaysia-period pattern team
provenance: Original Chang Hon composition.

meaning: 'Fifty-four steps': direct Korean reading of Gojushiho (五十四歩), the number 54 having Buddhist significance (half of 108); the kata's flowing, drunken-crane movements are among the most advanced in the Shuri-te canon.
name: O Sip Sa Bo
note: The highest classical karate-derived hyung in Moo Duk Kwan Tang Soo Do/Soo Bahk Do, deriving from Useishi/Gojushiho of the Matsumura-Itosu line as transmitted in Japanese karate. Korean recension of Gojushiho, taught at 4th dan and above.
origin_person: Shuri-te transmission via Sokon Matsumura and Anko Itosu
origin_place: Shuri, Okinawa; brought to Seoul, Korea

era: Created 1965-1967; adopted 1967; superseded by the new Koryo in 1972
meaning: 'Koryo' names the Goryeo dynasty (918-1392), from which the Western name 'Korea' derives, and the seonbae warrior-scholar spirit that repelled the Mongol invasions.
modifier: Superseded, not modified: the 1971-72 committee wrote an entirely new Koryo rather than revise this one
name: Old Koryo (Koryo Il Jang)
note: MISSING from the database, which holds only the 1972 'Koryo'. Two distinct forms share the name and this is a persistent source of confusion in the literature. DISPUTED: sources differ on whether the 1965-67 committee included Oh Do Kwan representation (Hyun Jong-myun is variously listed as Chung Do Kwan or Oh Do Kwan) and on whether the replacement in 1972 was technical or purely political, that is, to give the newly joined Moo Duk Kwan and Ji Do Kwan a stake in the curriculum. Superseded by the current Koryo but still taught in some kwan lines.
provenance: Original KTA composition, companion to the Palgwae series. Survives in Jung Do Kwan and other conservative lineages and in some overseas Chung Do Kwan schools; largely extinct in mainstream Kukki taekwondo.

introduced_by.name: Kukkiwon technical committee (individual authors not published)

meaning: 'The whole world'. Competition poomsae for competitors in their 50s and 60s.
name: Onnuri
note: MISSING from the database. Individual authorship unpublished. A further pair, Hanryu, is listed in some Kukkiwon competition documents alongside Bigak.

meaning: Trigram Gan (간, ☶), mountain. Ponderousness and stability; movement halted with finality.
name: Palgwae Chil Jang
note: MISSING as an individual entry. Seventh of the eight Palgwae. Same kwan-set completion as Palgwae Ee Jang.
provenance: Original KTA composition.

meaning: Trigram Tae (태, ☱), joyfulness, the lake. Firmness within, softness without; movements should be performed with inner calm and confidence.
name: Palgwae Ee Jang
note: MISSING as an individual entry. Six-man 1965-67 committee as for Palgwae Il Jang. Second of the eight Palgwae. Added chang-moo-kwan, chung-do-kwan, han-moo-kwan, ji-do-kwan, jung-do-kwan, song-moo-kwan. Internal inconsistency: 'Palgwae Il Jang' already carried the kwan ids and the umbrella 'Palgwae series' row carried chung-do-kwan and ji-do-kwan, but Ee Jang through Pal Jang carried only kukki-taekwondo/taekwondo. The Palgwae were composed in 1967 by the unified kwan committee before the 1971 Taegeuk replacement, so all eight belong to the same kwan set.
provenance: Original KTA composition, Shotokan-derived vocabulary.

era: Developed 1965-1967; adopted by the KTA 1967; superseded 1972
meaning: Trigram Keon (건, ☰), heaven and light, the pure yang. As the origin of all things it is the first and most basic of the set.
modified_era: Frozen in 1967; replaced by Taegeuk Il Jang in 1972
modifier: Retained unchanged by the ITF-independent Kukkiwon dissenters; never revised by the KTA, which replaced rather than amended the series
name: Palgwae Il Jang
note: MISSING as an individual entry: the database holds only an aggregate 'Palgwae series'. The 1965-67 committee is documented as Kwak Kun-sik (Chung Do Kwan), Park Hae-man (Chung Do Kwan), Hyun Jong-myun (Chung Do Kwan/Oh Do Kwan), Lee Yong-sup (Song Moo Kwan), Lee Kyo-yoon (Han Moo Kwan, then styled Yoon Moo Kwan) and Kim Soon-bae (Chang Moo Kwan). Note the correction to the current database: Lee Chong-woo did NOT sit on the 1965-67 committee. Moo Duk Kwan and Ji Do Kwan were unrepresented, which is precisely why the series was scrapped in 1971-72. [Verifier: Form, 1967 KTA adoption and committee membership all check out. But the modifier field is incoherent: 'ITF-independent Kukkiwon dissente First of the eight Palgwae. Added ji-do-kwan only, so that all eight Palgwae carry an identical kwan set. Ji Do Kwan is named on the file's own 'Palgwae series' umbrella row but was missing from Il J
origin_person: Korea Taekwondo Association poomsae committee (1965-67), chaired collectively by five kwans
provenance: Newly composed for the unified KTA curriculum, drawing on Shotokan-derived Chung Do Kwan and Song Moo Kwan basics. No Okinawan kata antecedent.

meaning: Trigram Seon (손, ☴), wind. Both gentle and destructive; humility and penetrating persistence.
name: Palgwae Oh Jang
note: MISSING as an individual entry. Fifth of the eight Palgwae. Same kwan-set completion as Palgwae Ee Jang.
provenance: Original KTA composition.

meaning: Trigram Gon (곤, ☷), earth, the pure yin. Receptivity and the nurturing ground on which everything takes root; the last of the gup-grade set, immediately before black belt.
name: Palgwae Pal Jang
note: MISSING as an individual entry. Many older Kukkiwon-lineage schools, particularly outside Korea, retained the full Palgwae set after 1972 and still teach it in parallel with the Taegeuk. Eighth and final Palgwae. Same kwan-set completion as Palgwae Ee Jang.
provenance: Original KTA composition.

meaning: Trigram Jin (진, ☳), thunder. Great power and dignity; danger met with courage.
name: Palgwae Sa Jang
note: MISSING as an individual entry. Fourth of the eight Palgwae. Same kwan-set completion as Palgwae Ee Jang.
provenance: Original KTA composition.

meaning: Trigram Ri (리, ☲), fire and the sun. Warmth, enthusiasm and hope.
name: Palgwae Sam Jang
note: MISSING as an individual entry. Third of the eight Palgwae. Same kwan-set completion as Palgwae Ee Jang.
provenance: Original KTA composition.

meaning: Trigram Gam (감, ☵), water. Ceaseless flow; hardship overcome by constancy.
name: Palgwae Yuk Jang
note: MISSING as an individual entry. Sixth of the eight Palgwae. Same kwan-set completion as Palgwae Ee Jang.
provenance: Original KTA composition.

meaning: 'Eight trigrams' (palgwae = bagua): eight forms keyed to the eight trigrams of the I Ching, from Keon (heaven) to Gon (earth), representing the full range of natural phenomena.
name: Palgwae series
note: The KTA's first unified coloured-belt set, drafted by a committee drawn from a subset of kwans (including Lee Chong-woo of Jidokwan and Lee Kyo-yoon of Hanmookwan, with Kwak Kun-sik, Hyun Jong-myun, Park Hae-man, Kim Soon-bae and others); because major kwans were unrepresented, an expanded committee replaced the set with the Taegeuk poomsae in 1971-1972, though many schools still teach Palgwae. Colour-belt curriculum of the early KTA.
variants: Palgwae Il Jang to Pal Jang

meaning: Pen name of Chong Mong-chu (1400), a loyalist poet and physicist of the Koryo dynasty, remembered for the line 'I would not serve a second master though I might be crucified a hundred times'. 36 movements; performed entirely along a straight line to symbolise unswerving loyalty.
name: Po-Eun
note: DISPUTED: one of the fifteen 1962-64 patterns claimed by Kim Bok-man and Woo Jae-lim as co-creations. Historical figure honoured: Jeong Mong-ju. First-dan pattern performed entirely on one line, honouring the Goryeo loyalist Jeong Mong-ju (Poeun). Second of the black-belt tul. Added itf-chang-ung, itf-choi-jung-hwa, itf-weiler, gtf. Second-dan tul.
origin_person: Choi Hong-hi with the Malaysia-period pattern team
provenance: Original Chang Hon composition.

meaning: 'Peace', the aspiration for reconciliation on the Korean peninsula, standing in the GTF canon roughly where Tong-Il stands in the ITF's.
name: Pyong-Hwa
note: MISSING from the database.
provenance: Original GTF composition.

meaning: 'Plain' or open plateau, the vast fertile land that sustains human life. The performance line traces the hanja 一, the single horizontal stroke of the plain.
name: Pyongwon
note: DISPUTED authorship as for Keumgang and Taebaek. Fourth-dan Kukkiwon poomsae from the original KTA black-belt set. Fourth of the nine black-belt poomsae.
provenance: Original KTA composition. Fourth dan poomsae.

era: Pinan created c. 1904-1907; in Korea from the mid-1940s
meaning: 'Peaceful confidence, first level'. Corresponds to Pinan Nidan in the Okinawan order (Itosu's second form), which Funakoshi reversed with Shodan; Tang Soo Do follows the Shotokan Heian order.
modifier: Hwang Kee, Won Kuk Lee and Byung Jick Ro (Korean renderings)
name: Pyung Ahn Cho Dan
native: 평안 초단 / 平安 初段
note: MISSING as an individual entry: the database holds only 'Pyung Ahn series'. DISPUTED on two counts. First, Itosu's authorship: he is universally credited with composing the Pinan c. 1904-07 for the Okinawan school system, but whether he composed them outright or broke down an older kata (commonly said to be Kusanku, or a Chinese form called Channan) is unresolved. Second, the Shodan/Nidan ordering swap means the Korean Cho Dan is Itosu's second form, not his first. [Verifier: Kata and Itosu attribution are right (c. 1904-1907, contested against the Channan precursor, so disputed=true is correct). Caveat: Funakoshi's 'renamed' role is only partly applicable, since the Heian renaming came with Korean recension of Pinan Shodan.
provenance: DERIVES FROM Pinan Shodan / Heian Shodan. Carried to Korea by Won Kuk Lee (from Funakoshi, Tokyo), Byung Jick Ro (also from Funakoshi, Tokyo) and adopted by Hwang Kee at Moo Duk Kwan.
sources: Mark Bishop, Okinawan Karate, Appendix C
Hwang Kee, Tang Soo Do (Soo Bahk Do), 1978

era: Created c. 1904-1907; in Korea from mid-1940s
meaning: 'Peaceful confidence' or 'safety and calm': the Korean reading of Pinan (平安), Itosu's name expressing that mastery of the five forms lets one defend oneself with a calm mind.
name: Pyung Ahn series
note: Itosu's five Pinan (drawn largely from Kusanku and Channan) reached Korea as Shotokan's Heian through Won Kuk Lee (Chung Do Kwan) and Byung Jick Ro (Song Moo Kwan), both Funakoshi students, while Hwang Kee learned them substantially from Japanese karate books; Yun Kwae-byung's Ji Do Kwan transmitted Shudokan/Shito-ryu versions. They remain the core geup forms of Tang Soo Do and early taekwondo. Korean recension of Itosu's Pinan series.
origin_place: Shuri, Okinawa; brought to Seoul, Korea
variants: Pyung Ahn Cho Dan to Oh Dan

The 'c. 1955-1965' era and 'Choi with early Oh Do Kwan instructors' attribution are unsourced, so disputed=false is over-confident: mark disputed=true.] Preparatory exercise, not a numbered tul.

meaning: 'Three-one', denoting 1 March 1919, the date of the Korean independence movement. 33 movements represent the 33 patriots who planned it.
name: Sam-Il
note: DISPUTED: one of the fifteen 1962-64 Malaysia patterns claimed by Kim Bok-man and Woo Jae-lim. Honours an event rather than an individual. [Verifier: Era is wrong. Sam-Il is one of the five patterns in Choi's 1959 Taekwon-Do Kyobon, so it predates the 1962-64 Malaysia period, and it does not appear in Kim Bok-man's Malaysia list. The Malaysia-team attribution (Kim Bok-man, Woo Jae-lim) therefore fails.] Third-dan Chang Hon pattern commemorating the Samil uprising against Japanese rule. Part of the sandan group of Chang Hon tul. Added itf-chang-ung, itf-choi-jung-hwa, itf-weiler, gtf. Third-dan tul.
origin_person: Choi Hong-hi with the Malaysia-period pattern team
provenance: Original Chang Hon composition.

meaning: Named for King Sejong the Great, who invented the Korean alphabet in 1443 and was a noted meteorologist. 24 movements represent the 24 letters of the Korean alphabet; the diagram represents the character for 'king'.
name: Se-Jong
note: DISPUTED. Named by Kim Bok-man as one of the five patterns in which he had lesser input. Historical figure honoured: King Sejong. Fifth-dan Chang Hon pattern honouring Korea's greatest monarch and his alphabet. Part of the godan group of Chang Hon tul. Added itf-chang-ung, itf-choi-jung-hwa, itf-weiler, gtf. Fifth-dan tul.
origin_person: Choi Hong-hi with the Malaysia-period pattern team
provenance: Original Chang Hon composition.

era: Seisan 17th-19th century; in Korea from the mid-1940s
meaning: 'Thirteen', usually explained as thirteen hands, thirteen techniques or thirteen postures. In Korean Shotokan-derived lineages also called Ban Wal ('half moon'), after Funakoshi's Hangetsu.
name: Sei Shan
note: MISSING from the database. DISPUTED: Seisan exists in mutually irreconcilable Naha-te, Shuri-te and Tomari-te versions and no originator can be named. The Korean form descends specifically from the Shotokan Hangetsu line, not from the Naha-te versions taught in Goju-ryu or Uechi-ryu. Some Tang Soo Do organisations list Sei Shan and Ban Wal as two forms, which is a naming artefact. Korean recension of Seisan.
origin_person: Origin unknown; among the oldest kata in the Okinawan repertoire, of Fujian Chinese derivation
origin_place: Naha and Shuri, Okinawa; ultimately Fujian
provenance: DERIVES FROM Seisan by way of Funakoshi's Hangetsu. Brought to Korea by Won Kuk Lee and Byung Jick Ro from Tokyo; taught by Hwang Kee in the Moo Duk Kwan dan syllabus.
sources: Mark Bishop, Okinawan Karate, Appendix C
Hwang Kee, Tang Soo Do (Soo Bahk Do), 1978

meaning: 'Reaching a level of purity of mind'. First-degree black belt form; 81 movements, that is 9 x 9.
name: Shim Jun
note: MISSING from the database. Level not verified against an ATA source in this session.
provenance: Original ATA composition. The nine black-belt forms culminate in the ninth-degree form of 99 movements.

era: Jitte 19th century; in Korea from mid-1940s
meaning: 'Ten hands': the Korean reading of Jitte (十手), traditionally meaning one who masters the kata fights with the strength of ten men.
name: Sip Soo
note: Derives from the Tomari-te kata Jitte as codified in Shotokan; in Moo Duk Kwan Tang Soo Do it is a dan-grade hyung noted for its slow, heavy pressing techniques and bo-defence interpretations. Korean recension of Jitte.
origin_person: Unknown; Tomari-te kata standardised through Itosu
origin_place: Tomari, Okinawa; brought to Seoul, Korea

meaning: 'Decimal', from the ten sipjangsaeng or symbols of longevity: sun, moon, mountain, water, stone, pine, herb of eternal youth, tortoise, deer and crane. The performance line traces the hanja 十 (ten).
name: Sipjin
note: DISPUTED. Beyond the authorship problem common to the yudanja set, some analysts argue that Sipjin borrows visibly from Okinawan kata known to the committee (the opening bull-block resembles motions in Jitte and the Shito-ryu Naha-te repertoire). The Kukkiwon presents all yudanja poomsae as wholly original Korean creations, which is a contested claim. Fifth-dan Kukkiwon poomsae from the original KTA black-belt set. Fifth of the nine black-belt poomsae.
provenance: Original KTA composition. Fifth dan poomsae; the most technically eclectic of the set, with several movements resembling Okinawan Naha-te shapes.
sources: comparative kata analyses in taekwondo historiography

meaning: Pen name of the great monk Choi Hyong-ung (1520-1604) of the Yi dynasty. 72 movements refer to his age when he organised a corps of monk soldiers with the help of his pupil Sa Myung Dang, and helped repel the Japanese pirates who overran most of the peninsula in 1592.
name: So-San
note: DISPUTED: one of the fifteen 1962-64 Malaysia patterns. Historical figure honoured: the monk Hyujeong (Seosan Daesa). [Verifier: Era and team wrong. So-San is likewise one of the four tul added in the 1972 textbook, not a Malaysia-period pattern, and Kim Bok-man does not claim it.] The longest Chang Hon pattern (72 movements), a fifth-dan tul honouring the warrior monk Seosan. Part of the godan group of Chang Hon tul. Added itf-chang-ung, itf-choi-jung-hwa, itf-weiler, gtf. Fifth-dan tul.
origin_person: Choi Hong-hi with the Malaysia-period pattern team
provenance: Original Chang Hon composition.

meaning: Second of the Songahm colour-belt forms; 23 movements.
name: Songahm Ee Jang
note: MISSING as an individual entry. Level not verified against an ATA source in this session.
provenance: Original ATA composition.

era: 1983 (Songahm forms introduced); system completed through the 1990s
meaning: 'Pine tree, rock', signifying evergreen strength on an immovable foundation. 18 movements, that is 2 x 9, nine being the significant number in the Songahm system (nine colour-belt grades, nine dan grades).
modified_era: Refined through the 1980s and 1990s; the full 18-form system settled by c. 1997
modifier: ATA technical committee under H.U. Lee
name: Songahm Il Jang
note: MISSING as an individual entry: the database holds only 'Songahm series'. Note that Haeng Ung Lee, the creator, is ABSENT FROM THE ROSTER despite being cited as the introducer in the existing kata row and as founder in the styles table. That is a clear roster gap. Level not verified against an ATA source in this session; the Songahm 1-5 set is unambiguously colour-belt material.
provenance: Original composition, written expressly to replace the karate-derived Chang Hon and Palgwae forms then taught in the ATA with a set presented as purely Korean. No Okinawan antecedent.
sources: ATA / Engage Martial Arts, 'Songahm Star & ATA Forms'

meaning: Fifth and last of the numbered Songahm colour-belt forms; 34 movements.
name: Songahm Oh Jang
note: MISSING as an individual entry. Level not verified against an ATA source in this session.
provenance: Original ATA composition.

meaning: Fourth of the Songahm colour-belt forms; 31 movements.
name: Songahm Sa Jang
note: MISSING as an individual entry. Level not verified against an ATA source in this session.
provenance: Original ATA composition.

meaning: Third of the Songahm colour-belt forms; 28 movements.
name: Songahm Sam Jang
note: MISSING as an individual entry. Level not verified against an ATA source in this session.
provenance: Original ATA composition.

meaning: 'Pine tree and rock': evergreen strength and unbreakable stability, the pen name concept of ATA founder Haeng Ung Lee; a proprietary set of coloured-belt forms (Songahm 1-5, In Wha 1-2, Choong Jung 1-2) and black-belt forms (Shim Jun onwards) designed so each rank's form uses only that rank's techniques.
name: Songahm series
note: The American Taekwondo Association replaced its earlier Chang Hon patterns with Haeng Ung Lee's Songahm system from 1983, one of the largest bespoke forms curricula outside the ITF and Kukkiwon canons; practised only within ATA/Songahm-affiliated bodies. Level not verified against an ATA source in this session.

meaning: Named for Queen Seondeok of Silla (reigned 632-647), the first reigning queen of Korea; the only GTF or ITF pattern honouring a woman.
name: Sun-Duk
note: MISSING from the database. Historical figure honoured: Queen Seondeok. Worth flagging because the entire 24-pattern ITF canon honours men only.
provenance: Original GTF composition.

meaning: 'Bright mountain', an ancient name for Mount Baekdu, where Dangun is said to have founded the Korean nation in 2333 BC. The performance line traces the hanja 工, signifying the link between heaven and earth made by man.
name: Taebaek
note: DISPUTED authorship as for Keumgang: Kukkiwon names no individual creator, and the current database attribution to Lee Chong-woo is anachronistic for a 1967 form. Third-dan Kukkiwon poomsae; its founding-myth reference parallels the ITF pattern Dan-Gun. Third of the nine black-belt poomsae.
provenance: Original KTA composition. Third dan poomsae.

meaning: Trigram Gan (간, ☶), mountain. Ponderousness and immovability; movements must stop cleanly and not be rushed. Introduces the tiger stance, scissor block and knee strike.
name: Taegeuk Chil Jang
note: Same nine-man committee. [Verifier: Same committee-list inconsistency. Era and modifier fine.] Seventh Taegeuk poomsae of the 1971 KTA committee set. Seventh of the eight Taegeuk; still a colour-belt form.
provenance: Original composition replacing Palgwae Chil Jang.

meaning: Trigram Tae (태, ☱), joyfulness and the lake. Inner firmness with outward softness; the poomsae should be performed serenely and with a smile.
name: Taegeuk Ee Jang
note: Same nine-man committee as Taegeuk Il Jang; the database currently names only two of them. [Verifier: Form and 1971-72 era are right, but the creator list silently drops Hyun Jong-myun and Lee Yong-sup, who are on the roster used for Taegeuk Il Jang. There is no source basis for per-form variation in committee membership; either use the full nine throughout or justify the difference.] Second of the eight Taegeuk geup poomsae created by the 1971 KTA committee. Second of the eight Taegeuk.
provenance: Original composition replacing Palgwae Ee Jang.

meaning: Trigram Keon (건, ☰), heaven and light, the pure yang and the source of creation. The first and most elementary poomsae.
modified_era: Kukkiwon Textbook editions from 1975; technical clarifications 1987, 2006 and later
name: Taegeuk Il Jang
note: CORRECTION to the current database, which credits only Lee Chong-woo and Lee Kyo-yoon. The 1971-72 Taegeuk committee was the six-man 1965-67 group plus three men brought in when Ji Do Kwan and Moo Duk Kwan joined the KTA: Lee Chong-woo (Ji Do Kwan), Bae Young-ki (Ji Do Kwan) and Han Young-tae (Moo Duk Kwan). Their inclusion is the whole reason the Taegeuk replaced the Palgwae. The Taegeuk set was created by the expanded KTA poomsae committee representing all major kwans (members documented include Kwak Kun-sik, Lee Chong-woo, Lee Kyo-yoon, Park Hae-man, Hyun Jong-myun, Kim Soon-bae, Lee Yong-sup, Han Young-tae and Bae Young-ki) and became the Kukkiwon/WT geup curriculum. First of the eight colour-belt Taegeuk.
origin_person: Korea Taekwondo Association poomsae committee (1971-72), the 1965-67 committee enlarged by Ji Do Kwan and Moo Duk Kwan representatives
provenance: Original composition, replacing Palgwae Il Jang. Technically simpler and more linear than the Palgwae it displaced.

meaning: Trigram Seon (손, ☴), wind. Wind is gentle but can become a hurricane; the poomsae alternates mild and forceful movements, introducing the elbow strike and hammerfist.
name: Taegeuk Oh Jang
note: Same nine-man committee. [Verifier: Same committee-list inconsistency; no source assigns individual Taegeuk forms to sub-groups of the committee.] Fifth Taegeuk poomsae of the 1971 KTA committee set. Fifth of the eight Taegeuk.
provenance: Original composition replacing Palgwae Oh Jang.

meaning: Trigram Gon (곤, ☷), earth, the pure yin. The receptive ground in which everything takes root and from which it grows. The final gup-grade poomsae before first dan.
name: Taegeuk Pal Jang
note: Same nine-man committee. The eight Taegeuk complete the cycle of the palgwae trigrams from pure yang to pure yin. [Verifier: Same committee-list inconsistency. Era and modifier fine.] Eighth and last Taegeuk poomsae of the 1971 KTA committee set, completing the eight-trigram cycle begun with Keon. Eighth and final Taegeuk.
provenance: Original composition replacing Palgwae Pal Jang.

meaning: Trigram Jin (진, ☳), thunder. Great power and dignity; thunder brings fear but is followed by calm, so the practitioner meets danger bravely.
name: Taegeuk Sa Jang
note: Same nine-man committee. [Verifier: Same inconsistent seven-name committee list as Ee/Sam Jang. Era 1971-72 and Kukkiwon Textbook revisions are fine.] Fourth Taegeuk poomsae of the 1971 KTA committee set. Fourth of the eight Taegeuk.
provenance: Original composition replacing Palgwae Sa Jang.

meaning: Trigram Ri (리, ☲), fire and the sun. Fire gives warmth, energy and hope; the poomsae introduces the knifehand strike and the alternating rhythm of heat and restraint.
name: Taegeuk Sam Jang
note: Same nine-man committee. [Verifier: Same defect: seven-name list, omitting Hyun Jong-myun and Lee Yong-sup without justification. Era and collective attribution otherwise fine.] Third Taegeuk poomsae of the 1971 KTA committee set. Third of the eight Taegeuk.
provenance: Original composition replacing Palgwae Sam Jang.

meaning: Trigram Gam (감, ☵), water. Water flows ceaselessly and adapts to any vessel; hardship is overcome by continuity. Introduces the roundhouse kick and outward palm block.
name: Taegeuk Yuk Jang
note: Same nine-man committee. [Verifier: Same committee-list inconsistency. Otherwise the 1971-72 dating and the collective KTA attribution hold.] Sixth Taegeuk poomsae of the 1971 KTA committee set. Sixth of the eight Taegeuk.
provenance: Original composition replacing Palgwae Yuk Jang.

meaning: Pen name of Yi Hwang (1501-1570), authority on Neo-Confucianism. 37 movements refer to his birthplace on the 37th parallel; the diagram represents the character for 'scholar'.
name: Toi-Gye
note: Historical figure honoured: Yi Hwang (Toegye). [Verifier: Real pattern (Yi Hwang). Absent from the 1959 book's five patterns and named in Kim Bok-man's Malaysia list; 1955-1959 and sole Choi/Nam authorship are contested, not settled.] Seventh Chang Hon pattern, honouring the philosopher Yi Hwang (Toegye). Seventh of the Chang Hon tul. Added itf-chang-ung, itf-choi-jung-hwa, itf-weiler, gtf. Seventh of the 24.
provenance: Original Chang Hon composition.

meaning: 'Unification', denoting the resolution to reunify Korea, divided since 1945. 56 movements; the diagram symbolises the homogeneous race.
name: Tong-Il
note: DISPUTED: one of the fifteen 1962-64 Malaysia patterns. Honours an aspiration rather than a person. The count of 24 tul is itself explained by Choi as the 24 hours of a day, one life. The final (sixth-dan) pattern of the Chang Hon system, closing the 24-tul cycle that Choi likened to the 24 hours of a day, one lifetime. Closes the ITF pattern set. Added itf-chang-ung, itf-choi-jung-hwa, itf-weiler, gtf. Sixth-dan tul, the last of the 24.
origin_person: Choi Hong-hi with the Malaysia-period pattern team
provenance: Original Chang Hon composition; the final and most demanding pattern of the 24.

meaning: Pen name of Syngman Rhee, first president of the Republic of Korea. 42 movements.
modified_era: Dropped from all subsequent editions after Rhee's fall in the April Revolution of 1960
name: U-Nam
note: DISPUTED. The pattern's very existence was for decades downplayed in ITF literature, and its content survives only in the 1959 book and in reconstructions. The claim that its movements were folded into Ko-Dang is asserted by some ITF historians but not documented by Choi. Politically it is the mirror image of the Juche episode: a pattern named for a head of state, deleted when that head of state fell. A rare, discontinued tul appearing in Choi Hong-hi's 1959 Korean-language book; it was quietly removed after Rhee's fall from power in 1960 and never entered the 24-pattern canon, surviving only through historical reconstruction.
provenance: Published in Choi's 1959 Korean-language Taekwon-Do textbook and then erased from the canon. Some ITF historians hold that its movements were recycled into Ko-Dang or Juche.

meaning: Named for General Ulji Mundok, who in 612 AD defeated a Tang (Sui) invading force of nearly one million with fewer than 10,000 men, using guerrilla tactics. 42 movements represent Choi Hong-hi's age when he designed the pattern; the diagram represents his surname.
name: Ul-Ji
note: DISPUTED on date as well as authorship. The internal 42-movement dating implies c. 1960, before Choi left for Kuala Lumpur, yet the pattern is usually grouped with the Malaysia set that Kim Bok-man claims to have co-created. Both cannot be straightforwardly true. [Verifier: Era wrong. Ul-Ji is one of the five patterns printed in the 1959 Taekwon-Do Kyobon, so it cannot date to c. 1960-1964, and it is not in Kim Bok-man's Malaysia-period list. The pattern itself is real (Ulji Mundeok).] Fourth-dan pattern honouring the victor of the Salsu River battle. The creator field reads 'Choi Hong-hi with his pattern team', which under-attributes. Nam Tae-hi (roster A0003) is specifically credited with designing three of the Chang Hon tul: Hwa-Rang, Choong-Moo and Ul-Ji. The dataset already names him on Hwa-Rang and Choong-Moo but not on Ul-Ji, which is an inconsistency rather than a judgement. Sugg
origin_person: Choi Hong-hi with his pattern team
provenance: Original Chang Hon composition. The 42-movement count dates the design precisely to c. 1960 given Choi's 1918 birth, which sits awkwardly with the 1962-64 Malaysia grouping.

era: Wanshu tradition 17th-19th century; in Korea from the mid-1940s
meaning: The Tang Soo Do name for Wanshu, after the Chinese envoy Wang Ji (Sappushi to Ryukyu, 1683), traditionally said to have demonstrated the form in Tomari. Known in Shotokan-derived Korean lineages as Empi or Yun Bi ('flying swallow').
modifier: Kosaku Matsumora and Chotoku Kyan (Okinawan versions); Gichin Funakoshi (Empi); Hwang Kee (Korean version)
name: Wang Shu
note: MISSING under this name: the database holds the same kata as 'Yun Bi' (the Chung Do Kwan / taekwondo name). Tang Soo Do and Soo Bahk Do call it Wang Shu, and the two names should be cross-linked rather than treated as separate forms. DISPUTED: the Wang Ji attribution is folklore, first recorded long after the fact, and there is no evidence the 1683 envoy taught any form. The Tomari and Shuri versions differ substantially. Korean recension of Wanshu.
origin_person: Traditionally the Chinese envoy Wang Ji; actual composer unknown
provenance: DERIVES FROM Wanshu / Empi. Brought to Korea by Won Kuk Lee and Byung Jick Ro from Shotokan and adopted by Hwang Kee for the Moo Duk Kwan dan syllabus.
sources: Mark Bishop, Okinawan Karate, Appendix C
Hwang Kee, Tang Soo Do (Soo Bahk Do), 1978
Shoshin Nagamine, The Essence of Okinawan Karate-do

meaning: Named for the monk Wonhyo (617-686), who popularised Buddhism in the Silla dynasty in 686 AD. 28 movements.
name: Won-Hyo
note: Historical figure honoured: the monk Wonhyo. Note the rare convergence with the Kukkiwon canon (Ilyeo), which otherwise shares no dedicatees with the ITF set. [Verifier: Real pattern. Same evidentiary problem: not among the 1959 book's five patterns, and named in Kim Bok-man's 15-tul claim. disputed must be true.] Fourth Chang Hon pattern; Wonhyo's oneness-of-mind philosophy also underlies the WT poomsae Ilyeo, a rare shared reference across the two systems. Fourth of the Chang Hon tul. Added itf-chang-ung, itf-choi-jung-hwa, itf-weiler, gtf. Fourth of the 24.
provenance: Original Chang Hon composition. The same monk is honoured by the Kukkiwon poomsae Ilyeo, whose diagram is the Buddhist manja.

introduced_by.name: Kukkiwon technical committee (individual authors not published)

meaning: 'Ambition'. Competition poomsae for competitors under 18.
name: Yamang
note: MISSING from the database. Individual authorship unpublished.
origin_person: Kukkiwon and Asian Taekwondo Union joint development committee
provenance: Newly composed competition poomsae.
sources: Kukkiwon / Asian Taekwondo Union announcement, September 2016

meaning: Named for Yon Gaesomun, the Goguryeo general who repelled the Tang invasion. 49 movements refer to the last two figures of 649 AD, the year he forced the Tang dynasty to quit Korea after destroying nearly 300,000 troops at Ansi Sung.
name: Yon-Gae
note: DISPUTED: one of the fifteen 1962-64 Malaysia patterns. Historical figure honoured: Yeon Gaesomun. [Verifier: Era and team wrong. Yon-Gae is one of the four tul added in the 1972 textbook (with Eui-Am, Moon-Moo, So-San) to complete the 24; it is absent from the 1965 twenty and from Kim Bok-man's Malaysia list, so 'Malaysia period, with Kim Bok-man and Woo Jae-lim' cannot stand.] Fourth-dan pattern honouring the Goguryeo military dictator who repelled Tang invasions. Part of the yondan group of Chang Hon tul. Added itf-chang-ung, itf-choi-jung-hwa, itf-weiler, gtf. Fourth-dan tul.
origin_person: Choi Hong-hi with the Malaysia-period pattern team
provenance: Original Chang Hon composition.

meaning: Named for General Kim Yu-sin, commanding general of the Silla dynasty. 68 movements refer to the last two figures of 668 AD, the year Korea was unified. The ready posture signifies a sword drawn to the right rather than the left, symbolising Kim's mistake of following the orders of his king to fight his own nation.
name: Yoo-Sin
note: DISPUTED: one of the fifteen 1962-64 Malaysia patterns. Historical figure honoured: Kim Yu-sin. Third-dan pattern honouring the unifier-general of Silla, with an unusually critical symbolism built into its start. Part of the sandan group of Chang Hon tul. Added itf-chang-ung, itf-choi-jung-hwa, itf-weiler, gtf. Third-dan tul.
origin_person: Choi Hong-hi with the Malaysia-period pattern team
provenance: Original Chang Hon composition.

meaning: 'Six paths, first level: Du Mun', the Great Gate. Yuk Ro means the six-fold path or six roads.
modified_era: Codified in his 1978 manual and in Soo Bahk Do Moo Duk Kwan Federation materials from 1976
name: Yuk Ro Cho Dan (Du Mun)
native: 육로 초단 두문 / 六路 初段 斗門
note: MISSING as an individual entry: the database holds only 'Yuk Ro series'. DISPUTED. Whether these forms genuinely reconstruct a Joseon-era art or are modern compositions loosely inspired by an illustrated text is contested. The Muye Dobo Tongji's kwon bup chapter contains static postures, not sequences, so the reconstruction is necessarily Hwang Kee's own interpretation. Presenting them as recovered Korean antiquity, as Moo Duk Kwan literature does, overstates the evidence. Derived by Hwang Kee from the Muye Dobo Tongji.
provenance: Original composition derived by Hwang Kee from the Muye Dobo Tongji (1790), the Korean royal military manual he obtained in 1957. The text does not fully describe the sequences; Hwang Kee expanded its illustrations into complete forms.
sources: Hwang Kee, Tang Soo Do (Soo Bahk Do), 1978
Capital Soo Bahk Do Academy, 'Yuk Ro Hyung Philosophy'

meaning: 'Six paths, second level: Joong Jyel', to cut the middle. Also romanised Joong Jol.
name: Yuk Ro Ee Dan (Joong Jyel)
native: 육로 이단 중절 / 六路 二段 中節
note: MISSING as an individual entry. Same reconstruction dispute as Yuk Ro Cho Dan. Second of the six Yuk Ro.
provenance: Original Hwang Kee composition from the Muye Dobo Tongji.
sources: Hwang Kee, Tang Soo Do (Soo Bahk Do), 1978

meaning: 'Six paths, fifth level: Sal Chu', the killing hammer.
name: Yuk Ro Oh Dan (Sal Chu)
native: 육로 오단 살추 / 六路 五段 殺捶
note: MISSING as an individual entry. Same reconstruction dispute. Fifth of the six Yuk Ro.
provenance: Original Hwang Kee composition from the Muye Dobo Tongji.
sources: Hwang Kee, Tang Soo Do (Soo Bahk Do), 1978

meaning: 'Six paths, fourth level: Yang Pyun', the high whip.
name: Yuk Ro Sa Dan (Yang Pyun)
native: 육로 사단 양편 / 六路 四段 揚鞭
note: MISSING as an individual entry. Same reconstruction dispute. Fourth of the six Yuk Ro.
provenance: Original Hwang Kee composition from the Muye Dobo Tongji.
sources: Hwang Kee, Tang Soo Do (Soo Bahk Do), 1978

meaning: 'Six paths, third level: Po Wol', to embrace the moon.
name: Yuk Ro Sam Dan (Po Wol)
native: 육로 삼단 포월 / 六路 三段 抱月
note: MISSING as an individual entry. Same reconstruction dispute. Third of the six Yuk Ro.
provenance: Original Hwang Kee composition from the Muye Dobo Tongji.
sources: Hwang Kee, Tang Soo Do (Soo Bahk Do), 1978

meaning: 'Six paths, sixth level: Choong Ro', to seize and capture. The final form of the series.
name: Yuk Ro Yuk Dan (Choong Ro)
native: 육로 육단 충로 / 六路 六段 衝路
note: MISSING as an individual entry. Same reconstruction dispute. The six Yuk Ro plus the seven Chil Sung and Hwa Sun form the specifically Korean core that distinguishes Soo Bahk Do from Tang Soo Do organisations that broke with Hwang Kee. Sixth and highest of the Yuk Ro.
provenance: Original Hwang Kee composition from the Muye Dobo Tongji.
sources: Hwang Kee, Tang Soo Do (Soo Bahk Do), 1978

era: Created from 1958, after Hwang Kee's 1957 discovery of the Muye Dobo Tongji
meaning: 'Six paths' or 'six-road' forms: six hyung (Du Mun, Jung Jul, Po Wol, Yang Pyun, Sal Chu, Choong Ro), each named for its governing concept, reconstructing indigenous-Korean-flavoured movement from classical texts.
name: Yuk Ro series
note: Created by Hwang Kee following his study of the Muye Dobo Tongji (1790 Korean military manual) found in the Seoul National University library in 1957; intended to root Soo Bahk Do in Korean rather than Japanese sources. The forms are modern creations inspired by the text, not reconstructions of surviving ancient forms. Hwang Kee's reconstruction from the Muye Dobo Tongji.
variants: Yuk Ro Cho Dan to Yuk Dan

meaning: Pen name of Yi I (1536-1584), the Neo-Confucian scholar called 'the Confucius of Korea'. 38 movements refer to his birthplace on the 38th parallel; the diagram represents the character for 'scholar'.
name: Yul-Gok
note: Historical figure honoured: Yi I (Yulgok). [Verifier: Real pattern (Yi I). Era 1955-1959 unsupported by the 1959 publication record; Kim Bok-man claims co-creation 1962-64. Contested attribution presented as settled.] Fifth Chang Hon pattern, honouring the neo-Confucian scholar Yi I (Yulgok). Fifth of the Chang Hon tul. Added itf-chang-ung, itf-choi-jung-hwa, itf-weiler, gtf. Fifth of the 24.
provenance: Original Chang Hon composition.

era: Wanshu 17th-19th century tradition; in Korea from mid-1940s
meaning: 'Flight of the swallow', from the darting, rising and dropping movements; the alternate Korean name Wang Shu preserves the older Okinawan title Wanshu, said to honour the Chinese envoy Wang Ji (1683).
name: Yun Bi
note: Reached Korea as Shotokan's Enpi (Funakoshi's rename of Wanshu); Tang Soo Do lineages use both Yun Bi and Wang Shu for essentially the same hyung. The Wang Ji origin story is tradition, not documented history. Korean recension of Enpi/Wanshu.
origin_person: Traditionally linked to the envoy Wang Ji; Tomari-te transmission
origin_place: Tomari, Okinawa; brought to Seoul, Korea

era: 1980s (style founded 1980; kata published in Fighting Karate, 1985)
meaning: Series names are functional Japanese: beginner's forms, basic forms, sparring forms, throwing forms and real-fight forms; together they encode Sabaki, the repositioning method of moving off-line to the opponent's blind side.
name: Ashihara kata series
note: Ashihara discarded the traditional Okinawan-Japanese kata canon of his Kyokushin upbringing entirely and composed these modern series so that every movement maps directly onto full-contact fighting at short, middle and long range, performable solo or with a partner. They are documented as kata by the style's own organisations and publications.

meaning: Named by grade rather than image: graded sequences expressing Enshin's circle-centre (enshin) principle, using Sabaki to convert an opponent's force by moving to the blind spot and unbalancing.

note: Ninomiya, Ashihara's former student, built Enshin's belt-graded kata on the same Sabaki logic as the Ashihara series rather than on classical forms; no kata named Junro is documented in Enshin (that name belongs to Tetsuhiko Asai's Shotokan series). The forms are documented in Enshin organisational material and style references.

meaning: reclining dragon
name: Garyu
note: Held with a person (line 31). The only Kyokushin kata in the WKF canon, and securely attributed. The only advanced Kyokushin kata with no Okinawan antecedent, created by Oyama and named after his pen name Garyu, itself the Japanese reading of the characters for Il Loong, the Korean village of his birth. It showcases Kyokushin-specific fighting technique including sacrifice moves and low sweeps. Named for Oyama's birthplace; not taught below black belt. Added ifk-kyokushin, iko-1, iko-3, kyokushin-budokai, shidokan. Oyama's own composition, named for his birthplace; unique to Kyokushin and retained across its branches.

meaning: 'To destroy, major'

Some commentators treat them as direct descendants of Miyagi's kata. The database should record both readings rather than silently merging with Gekisai dai ichi. [Verifier: Kyokushin sources describe Gekisai Sho as developed from Oyama's training under So Nei Chu rather than imported directly from Goju-ryu, and it sits at a much higher grade (1st kyu) than Goju's Gekisai Dai Ni. Equating it with Miyagi's 1940 form is contested, so keep disputed=true and add So Nei Chu.] The last brown-belt kata before shodan. meaning: 'To view the sky'
name: Kanku (Kyokushin)
note: Kyokushin's senior Shotokan-derived kata, the counterpart to its Goju-derived set, and evidence in the cladogram for Kyokushin's dual descent. DISPUTED: Oyama's Shotokan training is documented but its depth is contested, and the Kyokushin version differs from the JKA form in several sequences without any record of who made the changes. Kyokushin recension of Kanku Dai, reserved for senior black belts. Added iko-3, kyokushin-budokai, kyokushin-kan, shidokan, world-oyama. CANONICAL FORM: 'Kanku Dai'. Oyama took the kata from his Shotokan training under Funakoshi; the Kyokushin performance differs but the form is the same 観空.

meaning: 'Peaceful and safe, numbers one to five': Kyokushin retains Itosu's original Okinawan name Pinan rather than Funakoshi's rename Heian.

note: Oyama restructured the five Pinan with Kyokushin stances, circular blocks and Goju flavouring, and added ura versions performed with spinning turns, credited to him as a training method for balance and close fighting. The retention of the name Pinan signals Kyokushin's dual Shotokan-Goju parentage. Kyokushin's recension of the Heian/Pinan series. Added iko-1, ifk-kyokushin, iko-3, kyokushin-budokai. Kyokushin's rendering of the Itosu Pinan; universal across the kata-retaining Kyokushin bodies.

The Ura kata are Kyokushin's only structurally original contribution to the Pinan family and belong in the database as distinct entries from the held 'Pinan sono ichi-go'. Spinning versions, taught through the green and brown belt grades. Added iko-3, kyokushin-budokai. Same ura-kata caveat as Taikyoku Ura.

The same Goju channel supplied Kyokushin's Gekisai, Saiha (Saifa), Seienchin, Seipai and Tensho. Kyokushin adopted Sanchin from Goju-ryu but places it later than the Okinawan schools do. One of five 三戦 rows in the file; Oyama's version descends from the Goju line through So Nei Chu and Yamaguchi Gogen and belongs on the canonical entry as a variant.

meaning: 'Fifty-four steps': an alternative Japanese reading of the same characters as Gojushiho, the number 54 carrying Buddhist significance (half of 108, the number of worldly desires).
name: Sushiho
note: Oyama's rendering of Gojushiho (the old Useshi), reached via its Shotokan transmission and modified to Kyokushin body mechanics; the reading Sushiho distinguishes it from Shotokan's Gojushiho Dai and Sho. It sits among the highest kata of the Kyokushin canon. Kyokushin recension of Gojushiho; the longest kata in the Kyokushin canon. meaning: 'Grand ultimate, numbers one to three': the Kyokushin rendering of Funakoshi's Taikyoku, taught as the gateway to the style's kata canon.
name: Taikyoku sono ichi-san
note: Oyama, a direct student of Funakoshi, carried the Taikyoku into Kyokushin with modified stances and fighting emphasis, later adding ura (spinning) versions and the Sokugi (kicking) Taikyoku set unique to the Kyokushin lineage. They remain the first kata across nearly all Kyokushin offshoots. Kyokushin inherited the Taikyoku set from Shotokan as its beginner curriculum. Added iko-1, ifk-kyokushin, iko-3, kyokushin-budokai. The Kyokushin rows split into two inconsistent tagging habits: some carried the IKO/IFK set, others the Kyokushin-kan/Seido/World Oyama/Shidokan set, for kata that are in every one of those syllabi. Ashihara, Enshin, Seidokaikan, Byakuren and Zendokai are deliberately excluded throughout: those offshoots dropped the classical kata for their own sets, which the file already records separately.

name: Taikyoku sono ichi-san Ura
note: DISPUTED authorship, and the client should be told so plainly. The Ura kata are attributed to Oyama by the organisation, but no Kyokushin source names the individual who devised them, and several senior instructors of the 1960s honbu (Kurosaki among those named in oral accounts) have been credited informally. Record as honbu-developed under Oyama's direction. Spinning versions of the beginner kata, taught immediately after the originals. Added iko-3, kyokushin-budokai. Deliberately not given seido-juku or world-oyama: the ura kata are not uniformly retained outside the IKO/IFK/Shinkyokushin/Kyokushin-kan line.

meaning: 'Rotating palms' (or 'revolving hands'): soft circular open-hand movements over a Sanchin base, the yin counterpart to Sanchin's hardness.
name: Tensho (Kyokushin)
note: Oyama prized Tensho above all forms, writing that it was 'the most indispensable of the advanced kata' and the distillation of karate's hard-soft principle; it entered Kyokushin directly from his Goju-ryu training. The kata is Miyagi's composition, so its presence in Kyokushin is transmission, not creation. Kyokushin recension of Miyagi's kata. Added ifk-kyokushin, iko-1, iko-3, kyokushin-budokai, shidokan, world-oyama. CANONICAL FORM: 'Tensho' (existing naha-te row, which already lists kyokushin).

meaning: Usually written with characters read as 'safe three' and glossed in Kyokushin as 'to keep pure', striving to maintain integrity of principle under pressure; the etymology is debated.

It appears in no mainstream Okinawan syllabus outside these lines. A Kyokushin signature kata of uncertain origin. Added ifk-kyokushin, iko-1, iko-3, kyokushin-budokai, shidokan, world-oyama. A Kyokushin-specific southern kata, universal across the kata-retaining branches.
